paragraphs: Anthropic’s life sciences team is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: BigHat Biosciences , Bristol Myers Squibb , Divergence Labs , Enveda , Generate Biomedicines , and The Column Group . We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here .

There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like proposing initial designs for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more.

Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development.

We prove that, for some ﬁxed δ >0, one has ν(n) ≥ n1+δ for inﬁnitely many n. This disproves the well-known unit distance conjecture from [ Erd46]. The construction passes through an inﬁnite unramiﬁed tower of totally real number ﬁelds with 3-power Galois groups of growing degree, in which a ﬁxed set of rational primes splits completely. After adjoining i, these ﬁelds produce high-dimensional lattices with many elements whose images under every complex embedding have absolute value 1. Golod–Shafarevich theory ensures existence of an inﬁnite such tower, even after a quotient step making the prescribed Frobenius classes trivial. A crucial property of the construction is that all resulting discriminants and class numbers are at most exponential in the extension degree. 1 Main Result For a ﬁnite set P ⊂ R2, let ν(P ) = # {{x,y } ⊂ P : |x −y| = 1} andν(n) = max |P |=nν(P ). The planar unit-distance problem goes back to Erdős [ Erd46], who conjectured that there should be an absolute constant C such that, for all suﬃciently large n, ν(n) ≤n1+C/ log logn. (1) The same 1946 paper also introduced the distinct-distances problem, later resolved up to logarithmic factors by Guth–Katz [ GK15]. An elementary upper bound is ν(n) = O(n3/2): the Euclidean unit-distance graph is K2,3-free, since two unit circles meet in at most two points, and the Kővári–Sós–Turán theorem applies [ KST54]. The best known upper bound ν(n) = O(n4/3) is due to Spencer–Szemerédi–Trotter [ SST84]; Székely later gave a short crossing-number proof of this incidence bound [ Sze97]. It is useful to compare this with the same question for other norms on R2, a direction studied systematically by Brass [ Bra96]. records.title: Magnetar brings faster, simpler, quantum-ready zero-knowledge proofs
records.summary: Zero-knowledge proofs can verify computing results without rerunning workloads or exposing sensitive data. Magnetar helps bring them into the mainstream with support for standard programming languages, major speed gains, and quantum-resistant security. The post Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar appeared first on Microsoft Research .
records.rights_note: 本站保留结构化摘要与必要短摘录；完整内容请查看原始来源。
key_points: Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly.
Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run.

Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now.
Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges.
It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions.

records.summary: BACE treats generated code and tests as co-evolving populations instead of accepting synthetic tests as ground truth. Bayesian belief updates model tests as noisy sensors, while public examples anchor the search and reduce self-validating drift. key_points: BACE: LLM-based Code Generation through Bayesian Anchored Co-Evolution of Code and Test Populations Kaushitha Silva WSO2 Santa Clara, CA, USA kaushitha@wso2.com Srinath Perera WSO2 Santa Clara, CA, USA srinath@wso2.com Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in code generation.
While an interactive feedback loop can improve performance, writing effective tests is a non-trivial task.
Early multi-agent frameworks, such as AgentCoder, automated this process but relied on generated tests as absolute ground truth.
This approach is fragile: incorrect code frequently passes faulty or trivial tests, while valid solutions are often degraded to satisfy incorrect assertions.
Addressing this limitation, newer methods have largely abandoned test generation in favor of planning and reasoning based on examples.

sections.title: 摘要
sections.body: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in code generation. While an interactive feedback loop can improve performance, writing effective tests is a non-trivial task. Early multi-agent frameworks, such as AgentCoder, automated this process but relied on generated tests as absolute ground truth. This approach is fragile: incorrect code frequently passes faulty or trivial tests, while valid solutions are often degraded to satisfy incorrect assertions. Addressing this limitation, newer methods have largely abandoned test generation in favor of planning and reasoning based on examples. We argue, however, that generated tests remain a valuable signal if we model them as noisy sensors guided by Bayesian updates. We argue, conversely, that generated tests remain a high-value signal when modeled as noisy sensors within a Bayesian framework. By anchoring this search on minimal public examples, we effectively mitigate the co-evolutionary drift typical of self-validating loops. paragraphs: When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call.

We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded.

Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead.

sections.title: 摘要
sections.body: Reinforcement learning (RL) trained language model agents with tool access are increasingly deployed in coding assistants, research tools, and autonomous systems. We introduce the Reward Hacking Benchmark (RHB), a suite of multi-step tasks requiring sequential tool operations with naturalistic shortcut opportunities such as skipping verification steps, inferring answers from taskadjacent metadata, or tampering with evaluationrelevant functions. RHB supports independent and chained task regimes, where chain length acts as a proxy for longer-horizon agent behavior. We evaluate 13 frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and DeepSeek. Exploit rates range from 0% (Claude Sonnet 4.5) to 13.9% (DeepSeek-R1-Zero), varying sharply by posttraining style. A controlled sibling comparison (DeepSeek-V3 vs. DeepSeek-R1-Zero) shows RL post-training is associated with substantially higher reward hacking (0.6% vs. 13.9%), with consistent gaps across all four task families. We identify six exploit categories and find that 72% of reward hacking episodes include explicit chain-ofthought rationale, suggesting models often frame exploits as legitimate problem-solving. Simple environmental hardening reduces exploit rates by 5.7 percentage points (87.7% relative) without degrading task success. Models with near-zero exploit rates on standard tasks show elevated rates on harder variants, suggesting that production-aligned post-training appears to suppress reward hacking only below a complexity threshold where honest solutions remain tractable. 1Independent Researcher. Gemini 4 Argon is a step forward in what models can do — especially when it comes to deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. Its cyberdefense capabilities are frontier-level and designed to give defenders an advantage over attackers. To maximize its potential, we first wanted cyber defenders to put it to work via our Fairwind Program , while our own security teams used it to scan critical systems inside and outside of Google.

This window of limited access showed why these capabilities matter. For instance, Wiz used Argon to uncover a critical bug in hospital software that previous models had missed, helping protect hundreds of thousands of patient records. Meanwhile, Google’s own security teams used Argon to find and patch bugs across internal software or open-source software. This included fixing foundational vulnerabilities affecting systems globally, which are going through our responsible disclosure process.

records.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations - Microsoft Research
records.summary: Flint-interactive gives AI agents a language for creating interactive visualizations. Click a chart, filter data, highlight related content, and explore beyond the view the author originally chose. The post Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations appeared first on Microsoft Research .
records.rights_note: 本站保留结构化摘要与必要短摘录；完整内容请查看原始来源。
key_points: Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions.

Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators.

Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations.

records.title: Called to serve: Tech, research, and positive impact - Microsoft Research
records.summary: Lab Director Chris White has worked on research challenges with real-world implications—from new approaches to wartime data analysis to tools for combating human trafficking. key_points: In the summer of 2010, postdoc Chris White worked with a multidisciplinary team at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, to determine if a new approach to data analysis could prevent violence and protect troops during the war in Afghanistan.
At the conclusion of the program, the agency asked White to prove the value of his work—on the ground.

In this episode, Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu talks with White, director of Catalyst Lab at Microsoft Research, about his unexpected break from academic research to help lead advanced tech operations in Afghanistan and his later decision to again work on tech with immediate, real-world implications: dark-web search tools used to help…
Liu and White explore the influences that led to these experiences plus the important role of problem selection in innovation and remaining hopeful after seeing the darkest parts of humanity.
CHRIS WHITE: I have seen a lot of really bad humanity.
